The persistent storage systems built upon Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) demand a new form of memory consistency to ensure that, following a system crash and subsequent reboot, all software in review can correctly restore to a coherent state by either executing recovery procedures or halting operations. We are introducing a novel software approach called Algorithm-Directed Crash Consistency (ADC), a new standard of memory consistency tailored for the Persistent Memory Model (PMM). The ADC Memory Model (ADMM) is a component of this method, providing software tools to achieve ADC compliance by marking specific memory operations as volatile or restricting access to linear memory, thereby enabling the detection of inadmissible execution paths. We are also including a deadlock avoidance strategy to prevent the system from becoming stuck during recovery processes. In the context of high-performance computing, we are evaluating ADC on an NVM system with software implementing the PMM model, by comparing it to a conventional approach based on the traditional Disk Model (DM). We are finding that ADMM's ability to detect inadmissible execution paths surpasses DM's, while its impact on the system's execution path admissibility after a crash is superior to the impact introduced by the standard recovery methods associated with PMM.

Complex organizations like the Wikipedia article network rely on a structured knowledge representation, modeled through a DAG of submodule levels. The creation of such a framework, however, poses a computational challenge, where an optimal method for generating the complete organization hierarchy is an unsolved problem. Although a near-optimal polynomial-time algorithm exists for computing individual submodules, the efficiency of generating the entire hierarchy is unknown. To address this gap in knowledge, researchers compared the efficiency of four polynomial methods for generating hierarchical representations: level-order traversal, topological sorting, integrating Karp's algorithm, and aggregating individual computations. These methods were evaluated through both theoretical analysis and empirical testing, where additional constraints like minimizing link disruptions or grouping article subsets were also considered.

This paper reevaluates the flux-driven statistical prediction of the three-body problem using Monte Carlo simulations. Previous studies have proposed a four-parameter model based on energy conservation, but our research demonstrates that incorporating flux as a dominant factor leads to a more accurate prediction, largely resulting in a narrow, consistent distribution of3N. Specifically, our findings confirm the flux-driven statistical prediction of the three-body problem, which predicts a power-law distribution of high-precision escape rates of pre-embedded unbound orbits, characterized by two parameters: a scale rate and a scale energy.

The experiment analyzed the suppression of prompt and non-prompt charmonia in Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon-pair of 5.02 TeV by employing the D*--J/ψ mesons. Utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC, the measurement involved comparing the yield ratios of prompt J/ψ and ψ(2S) mesons in Pb-Pb collisions to those in pp collisions. Results revealed that both prompt J/ψ and ψ(2S) mesons were suppressed in Pb-Pb collisions, with the suppression factor decreasing as the number of interacting binary nucleon pairs decreased at centralities with high Pb-Pb collision density. In Pb-Pb collisions, the suppression factor was observed to be lower for ψ(2S) than for J/ψ mesons. In contrast, no significant difference was found in the suppression factors between J/ψ and ψ(2S) mesons when considering non-prompt yields. These findings are consistent with predictions from theoretical models.

We suggest a robust framework to convert any first-order logic with continuous metrics into a distinct, metric-based language. Our construction is specifically tailored to the metric aspect of the logic, differing from traditional approaches that focus on syntree structures. As a consequence, our method reveals a correspondence between metric arguments in Stone duality and a transformation of the logic itself. Furthermore, our framework enables a precise representation of the functorial relationship between metric spaces and their corresponding metric theories.

To systems engineering test suites generate an enormous number of test cases, 
resulting in prolonged execution times and resource wastage. In view of this challenge, 
researchers have developed an algorithm for singular value decomposition (SVD) to efficiently 
select test cases. The proposed approach involves a co-processing method where large datasets are divided 
into sub-matrices and processed in parallel to identify critical test cases. The parallel execution time of this strategy significantly reduces compared to traditional SVD, 
ensuring a balanced workload distribution and optimal performance.

A study has been conducted to address the complex issue of predicting and detecting suicidal ideation in individuals. By utilizing deep learning on a multi-source dataset that includes free-text, audio, and video recordings from two distinct sources, researchers aimed to create an effective predictive model. The integration of sequential data such as speech and video requires a combined approach, where the analysis of spoken words and non-verbal cues work together to identify patterns. A novel neural network architecture, consisting of recurrent units and a bidirectional convolutional layer, was developed to process speech, while video features were modeled using a recurrent unit and a unidirectional convolutional layer. By combining these features and applying recurrent embeddings, the model can effectively identify behaviors associated with suicidal ideation. In order to assess its performance, the model was evaluated using multiple metrics, including the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, precision, recall, and the F1 score. Notably, the model demonstrated an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.85, 0.83, and 0.84 for the entire dataset, as well as for two separate datasets, obtained from free-text, audio, and video recordings, respectively.

As a benchmark pulsar wind nebula, Cassiopeia A offers valuable insights into the operation of pulsar magnetospheres and particle acceleration at pulsar magnetospheric boundaries, with its X-ray emission originating from PNe material interacting with the pulsar wind. Previous observations have provided estimates of polarization degree and angle, although uncertainty remains due to the varied nature of the spectrum. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the polarization properties of Cas A across the 15-80 keV energy range, using data from the Imager for X-ray Polarimetry Experiment. As an internal calibration source, the high polarization expected from Cas A will help validate the performance of the IXPE telescope.

The Erdos unique partitions problem seeks the smallest q value, such that any set of numbers under q^2, generated by a polynomial with integer coefficients and constant term zero and q as its highest degree coefficient, produces distinct sums when its degrees from one to two are combined. It has been proven that three is the smallest q value. In this study, we examine whether there are any q values, greater than three, that fail to meet this condition in the context of these specific two-variable sequences.

The sound speed of dense matter within small-radius stars is investigated in two distinct scenarios: one with non-strangonic quark matter and the other with quark matter. By examining this sound speed, we aim to gain insights into the dense matter composition inside small-radius stars and thus improve the constraints on unknown constants in various equations of state. We also explore the potential implications of this sound speed on compact star properties, including mass-radius relationships, and consider how it affects the minimum mass of such stars. Our findings indicate that dense matter composition inside small-radius stars might not necessarily involve non-strangonic quark matter.

The impact of compression and displacement on the thermal state of a harmonic oscillator has been investigated, revealing a new type of thermal state generated by compressing the vacuum under displacement, known as the compass state. This state, which lies on a manifold formed by alternating points of zero and maximum occupation probability, has maximum efficiency in extracting work from the oscillator. Notably, the compass state retains remnant thermal features, such as non-diagonal density matrix elements decaying exponentially, even after displacement. However, it loses its non-Gaussian character and becomes indistinguishable from a Gaussian mixed state under certain conditions, occurring when the displacement variance exceeds the compression-related occupation, exhibiting non-Gaussianity.

To the best of our knowledge, this study introduces a novel approach to characterizing complex interface geometries using skeletons. Our method preserves the intrinsic features of a given multiphase flow while capturing its overall pattern through a simplified representation. Our research involves creating skeletons for two-dimensional multiphase flows consisting of K components, where each component forms a separate, smooth phase within a square domain. Given the arrangement of these phases, our approach generates a skeleton along with associated skeletons for each individual phase. We present a mathematical existence proof for this skeleton structure, outlining its key properties. Additionally, we develop an algorithm to compute the skeleton numerically, leveraging its connection to critical points of a specially constructed vector field. Our method enables efficient computation of a skeleton through the analysis of stationary points and a corresponding flow along these points. Our work also includes a framework for defining and calculating quantitative descriptors of multiphase structures using the skeleton. These descriptors serve as useful tools for tracking changes over time in time-dependent multiphase flows. Our research showcases the effectiveness of this approach through various test cases, where our method successfully produces coherent skeletons that accurately reflect the overall structure of complex configurations. Our framework proves to be computationally efficient, robust, and straightforward to apply.

Self-rotating viruses are made up of symmetric subunits arranged in a specific pattern, where the arrangement on the outer layer differs from the inner layers. This specific structure enables the virus to rotate on its own without external forces. To understand how this unique structure forms, researchers applied a novel theoretical framework based on the interaction forces between the virus's building blocks. They treated the virus's subunits as soft spheres that can pack together in different ways, where the specific arrangement is determined by the strength of their interactions. This new theoretical approach, or force model, can also explain the formation of another type of structure called self-assembled helical capsids.

In recent decades, the phenomenon of warped disk galaxies has become increasingly studied. A classification system is introduced to categorize these warps, ranging from types S to U. We focus on the most extreme warps of type U to explore their characteristics. A group of 31 such galaxies is examined using data from the SDSS, including photometry, spectra, and, for some, photometric velocity fields. Additionally, we analyze HST images for 8 of these galaxies to detect star-forming tidal arms, often found in "Jellyfish" star systems. We also examine the spatial distribution of these warped galaxies within the local universe. The newly classified warps exhibit distinct properties. The most severe warps, classified as type U, share common traits: they are found frequently in groups and clusters, often display star-forming tidal arms, and are associated with "Jellyfish" star systems. These systems are characterized by star-forming tidal arms extending from the galaxy disk into the halo. The most severe warps are linked to these systems, suggesting their disk disturbances result from ram-pressure effects as the galaxy moves through the intra-group or intra-cluster medium. This process also explains the group and cluster preferential found of these warped galaxies, as their disruption is size-dependent with smaller galaxies more prone to disk distortion.

We have demonstrated that under the condition of a bounded, smooth function representing the scalar curvature on a Ricci shrinker, any such instance is identical to the Gaussian example. Consequently, we derived that the curvature's growth on a Ricci shrinker is constrained.

Although Kudos et al. discovered a chiral elastic wave in the Pyrite structure of $Cr_{2}O_{3}$, further experimental evidence for this phenomenon is still lacking. A computational study has identified a material with the Laves structure, composed of K/Cs/rubidium (Rb) and Bi, which exhibits a chiral phonon despite having the spatial symmetry required for this wave. Chiral elasticity can still occur in this system due to the presence of cubic symmetry and can be experimentally verified through neutron scattering, which is crucial for validating its existence. Additionally, the third harmonic generation would be unidirectional in this material, with an energy efficiency advantage over materials with broken symmetry. Chiral phonon-based spin-phonon coupling may also lead to the emergence of spin waves with topological properties in magnetic versions of this material.

In the context of metals, born effective loads play a crucial role in determining how nonthermal friction affects the damping of macroscopic supercurrent. A specific type of Born effective load, referred to as the nonadiabatic one, affects this in addition to the conventional adiabatric load. The concept of born effective loads has been expanded to apply to insulators with dynamical dipole transitions and how it relates to the infrared activity of phonons. Furthermore, a key distinction has been identified between the properties of born effective loads in insulators and those in metals. The current research also looks into how the nonadiabatic Born effective load arises in a specific type of metal, namely those with s-d hybridization, and how it affects the Drude weight in such metals.

To determine how dissipation in non-isothermal fluid turbulence is affected by
thermal fluctuations, researchers have used the idealized mixing-length model.
By analyzing three types of turbulence - isothermal, homogeneous temperature
fluctuations, and random temperature fluctuations, they found that different
thermal disturbance patterns affect dissipation in distinct ways.

A comprehensive description of magnetoelectric behavior in topological insulators is presented, incorporating the concept of magnetoelectric influence, an concept previously overlooked. Mathematical equations are developed to describe the influence of magnetoelectricity in the insulator's bulk and at its surface. An effective field theory is constructed to encompass all possible topological responses of the insulator, resulting in a set of three theoretical effects: magnetoelectricity, the Witten effect, and a half-integer quantum Hall effect. These phenomena can be experimentally distinguished through specific measurements of second harmonic polarization, the response to a free charge within the insulator, and the Hall conductivity on the insulator's surface.

In systems featuring delayed feedback, it's possible to completely control the level of chaotic diffusion. Our research focuses on a simple delay system where the time it takes to respond is comparable to the time it takes for the system to exchange information. By fine-tuning this delay time, the rate of diffusion in the system can increase dramatically, offering a new method for managing chaos in complex systems with time delays.

This paper examines behaviorally equivalent types of lambda calculus random lambda-calculus terms, focusing on almost sure properties. It proposes and demonstrates a semantic framework based on measure-theoretic continuous lattices with submeasures, providing a foundation to study properties of the random lambda calculus by assigning meaningful interpretations to random functions. It is shown that this semantics accurately models equivalence in both the untyped and strongly typed lambda calculuses, with a subsequent investigation into its connection to probabilistic semantics, notably relating equivalence to inclusion and exploring connections with other known results.

Our approach to analyzing engineering design discussions involves extracting key knowledge from the discussions using machine learning, specifically focusing on non-tabular data like free-form text, which is crucial for capturing the nuances of these conversations. By this method, discussions are viewed as virtual minds, reflecting collective problem-solving efforts. By extension, the knowledge extraction process can be seen as the emergence of a true collective intelligence. As a starting point, our model for extracting key knowledge from these discussions relies on conclusion stability as a measure. This measure assesses the overlap between the top knowledge contributions from multiple runs of the model, helping to determine its reliability and accuracy. To determine the right level of control for the model, we conducted experiments by adjusting the model's sensitivity to its parameters, specifically using ROUGE scores to determine the optimal settings for the parameters in question. This was done for two design communities, using a Unigram model and various configurations of BERT-based models, enabling us to draw broader conclusions about the stability and reliability of the knowledge extraction process.

Hawking-Elitzur-Polchinski no-cloning theorems pose challenges to theories attempting to unify quantum mechanics with general relativity, as they suggest Hawking radiation destroys information from black holes, contradicting the principles of general relativity. We propose that gravity, holographic vacuum fluctuations, and the post-inflation quantum field fluctuations behave as an integrated entity, where the macro-quantum-coherent state of the Higgs field interacts with the U(1) Goldstone bosons, giving rise to the force of gravity. This, in turn, enables the entanglement of infalling matter with the radiation, preserving the information, and thus resolving the black hole information paradox. As a result, the fundamental principles of both quantum mechanics and general relativity remain intact.

Several non-convex optimization algorithms inspired by proximal gradient methods have been used to solve problems in manifold optimization. However, these algorithms often converge slowly due to their linear convergence rates. In this paper, we propose an optimization algorithm on convex matrix and flow networks that utilizes Newton method, tailored for use with proximal gradient algorithms. Our method utilizes the dual problem formulation to compute Newton direction, which is then used to compute a more accurate descent direction. We show that this method maintains global convergence while achieving a linear convergence rate under convexity assumptions, and we adapt the algorithm for use on manifold optimization.

In a commutative ring with a nonzero multiplicative identity, we examine the concept of feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals. We demonstrate that in such rings, every feebly 1-absorbing prime ideal is minimal with respect to a specific property related to ideal containment. Furthermore, we explore the properties of feebly 1-absorbing prime ideals in specific types of rings, including local rings, hyperlocal rings, commutative affine algebras over a field, and certain types of ideals in these rings.

A novel method featuring event-by-event particle mass reconstruction is introduced for analyzing semileptonic B-meson decays using hadonic B-meson rebound baryon information. By utilizing full B-meson rebound baryon information, new possibilities are created to enhance signal separation and monitor systematics in semileptonic B-meson decay analyses. The current approach is demonstrated in studies of B-meson decays into the two-particle final state using simulated data. The demonstration involves using rebound baryon information to calculate mass-constrained likelihoods and verify that this method yields reliable results. Furthermore, the method is shown to provide accurate background suppression in mass distributions of B-meson decays into the three-particle final state using real data from the Belle II experiment. The demonstration involves using rebound baryon information in 2019-2021 Belle II data to calculate mass-constrained likelihoods and present mass distributions of B-meson decays into the three-particle final state of the $\rho$-vector meson.

Recently, photometric spectral reconstruction techniques have gained significant attention, yet they face a fundamental issue - they cannot be used for exoplanet exosphere spectroscopy because their resolution is insufficient. To overcome this limitation, our research proposes a solution involving custom-built, high-resolution spectrometers with customized slits and a novel remedy for cross-correlation methods in spectroscopy.

In the search for new medications, the considerable time expenditure is concentrated in identifying promising drug candidates from a vast library of inactive compounds. A key element of this process is assessing drug pairs to identify those with dual therapeutic applications. Current approaches to this problem include proprietary machine learning models and knowledge-based systems that leverage knowledge graphs. While effective, these models examine the issue through disparate lenses. By unifying these approaches and learning from the structured knowledge within knowledge graphs, we can develop a more cohesive and adaptable framework for pair scoring that can be applied broadly and optimized using adaptive learning techniques. We present such a unified relational deep learning framework, incorporating multiple scoring mechanisms and parameter optimizations, and compare our results from extensive experiments on three large datasets with state-of-the-art methods, showcasing our approach as a versatile and high-performing solution for new drug development and repurposing efforts.

Identifying damaged roads is a challenging task for experts due to the vast amount of road images and the diverse visual appearances of road defects. A significant issue arises when new countries or regions are considered, as their road conditions vary significantly, requiring the development of specialized detection models from scratch. This process is time-consuming and costly. A practical solution involves utilizing a general-purpose deep learning model that can effectively analyze road defects across different countries. A dataset was compiled with road images from multiple countries to train a general defect detection model, allowing it to be applied to road maintenance in a Spanish city. A thorough evaluation compared the results of various deep learning approaches, including the performance of a model fine-tuned on a set of road images with defect labels in Spain.

I'm introducing a novel approach to skill acquisition by observing actions taken in a different environment. This method, termed Cross-Domain Imitation Learning, enables the extraction of action principles from visible behaviors in another setting, which can be applied to control an agent in the original environment. CDIL utilizes observational data solely, eliminating the need for explicit task demonstrations. It's relevant for scenarios where direct observation is impractical due to cost, and it builds upon existing techniques for learning from indirect information. This paper outlines the Cross-Domain Imitation Learning framework and proposes two novel algorithms that achieve results comparable to state-of-the-art methods in skill acquisition.

In early cosmic history, the formation of low-mass objects is predicted to occur within disky accretion flows surrounding Population III stars.  These accretion disks are thought to shrink and vanish as they transition through resonance instabilities at a rate of around 10 to 100 years.  Previous research suggests that magnetic field effects play a crucial role in this process and could potentially cause resonance instabilities to eliminate fragmentation in Population III stars.  To test this idea, this study runs high-resolution simulations with a larger numerical domain to assess the influence of magnetic field strength on early object formation at various spatial and temporal scales.  The findings indicate that an extremely strong magnetic field, around -600 micro-Gauss, is necessary to trigger resonance instabilities and suppress fragmentation.  However, typical magnetic field effects within these simulations result in the creation of one high-mass object at the center of the simulated volume, surrounded by several marginally fragmented objects.  The research implies that magnetic field effects do not play a crucial role in suppressing early object formation and forming the first star clusters.

This work delves into the connection between redundancy, deduction, and association rules, focusing on link association rules with unitary bodies. It establishes that two such rules are linked by redundancy only when their antecedent and consequent parts are mutually associated. Full redundancy implies one is the inverse of the other. We also explore the concept of minimum-size bases, relating associations to perfect mappings and determining relationships for local and global redundancy. We prove that a minimum-size base exists, relate it to link and association rules with non-unitary elements, and offer a size bound.

A widely acknowledged problem within the US criminal justice system is the high prevalence of mental illness among convicted individuals.  Current research lacks a comprehensive understanding of how the criminal justice system addresses mental health.  Our study investigates the impact of mandatory therapy following conviction on crime rates and compliance with court orders.  Using an exclusive dataset that tracks Florida drivers convicted of DUI between 2005 and 2015, our analysis leverages a natural experiment based on a policy change.  This policy alteration resulted in the assignment of mandatory mental health counseling.  Our findings show that being subjected to mandatory therapy significantly lowers subsequent crime rates, particularly among female drivers and those who had prior convictions.  In contrast, being subjected to mandatory therapy has no measurable effect on compliance with other court orders.  However, a heterogeneity analysis reveals that individuals assigned to mandatory therapy who previously demonstrated non-compliance with other court orders were more likely to comply with specific restrictions, including the interdict on consuming alcohol.  These results imply that mandatory mental health counseling could be a beneficial component of the US criminal justice system, although the determination of who should receive it, and which other justice system offenders could benefit from it, requires further study.

This study derives novel types of parametric Apostol-Bernoulli numbers and polynomials, defines them, and examines their key characteristics using the complex variable method. It also establishes distinct types of relationships among these new entities and creates several notable identities as a result.

Radio map estimation is emerging as a promising technique for site-specific wireless network planning and optimization, wherein unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) collect measurements to generate a statistical representation of the environment's channel conditions. By analyzing these measurements, key parameters such as path loss and spatial correlations can be estimated, enabling operators to identify optimal locations for base stations and assess the coverage capabilities of wireless networks. In radio map estimation, a key challenge lies in collecting measurements from a two-dimensional area, which can be efficiently achieved by deploying swarms of autonomous UAVs. By utilizing inter-UAV and UAV-to-ground communication links, the swarms can synchronize their data collection process and efficiently cover the area of interest while minimizing travel time. This paper presents a novel approach to facilitate area coverage and coordination of swarms of UAVs, as well as an algorithm for three-dimensional path planning that allows the swarm to efficiently explore two-dimensional areas and collect radio measurements. The proposed method has been successfully tested through agent-based simulations, which utilize a micro air vehicle platform, and the effectiveness of this approach is evaluated through simulation results.

This paper introduces a novel, unsupervised machine learning approach for real-time Anomaly Identification on complex systems. The Anomaly Identification algorithm is built upon an Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that utilizes gauge likelihood analysis, taking into consideration the temporal and interdependent relationships of system states during the normal operation. An absolute and relative distance measure is employed to detect system deviations, and the method is demonstrated on a virtual aircraft flight data, yielding a 98.8% accurate result compared to the gold standard test data. Additionally, the model exhibits robustness in handling noisy and incomplete data.

This research delves into the area of individual authentication, utilizing sound and visual data from both captured images and thermal images through a thermal camera. Our approach combines three distinct modalities - audio, visual, and thermal - to create a robust verification system. While individual modalities can be used for identification, their combination proves even more effective. This study evaluates the performance of each modularity on a public dataset known as VCTK, which features audio-visual-thermal recordings of 315 individuals. Our findings demonstrate that the thermal modularity is particularly valuable, especially in scenarios where audio and visual data may not be accessible. Conversely, the combination of all three modalities yields the highest accuracy for individual verification.

Infinitely created, synthetic training data is generated by making minor alterations to existing real-world data. For translation tasks, these alterations involve modifying the text's syntax or vocabulary while preserving its original meaning. Similar approaches have been proposed for speech recognition, for example by altering the speech audio while preserving its underlying message. We explore the effect of such data augmentation on speech-based tasks and find that these modified samples can be created with almost no computational effort. We observe that the benefits are most pronounced when working with shorter speech sequences.

When a random sample cannot be obtained from a mixed distribution of possible populations, researchers often have access to independent observations of an associated auxiliary variable. These auxiliary variables can provide additional information and can be used to make inferences about the underlying parameters, specifically their average value, even without a random sample. A maximum likelihood approach has been developed to estimate the average parameter value, proving to be effective and efficient in simulations. This approach is implemented in the R software package hyperSample, available on the CRAN repository.

Achieving dependent attribute privacy in data releases often requires releasing artificially modified data. This modification process typically involves adjusting values, but does not account for changes in relationships between variables, which can expose private information. To address this, we enhance the definition of one-sided differential privacy to consider changes in variable relationships and establish a fundamental limit on minimizing exposure for private information. This framework depends on concepts such as joint entropies and conditional mutual information, relying on the assumption that the releasing entity has access to a probability distribution consistent with observed data from multiple data subjects. We demonstrate that achieving optimal privacy requires generating independent samples from this distribution. Moreover, we examine specific mechanisms, like modified synthetic data and partial regression mechanisms, within our framework and establish theoretical bounds for their privacy exposures.

We present new gas and dust maps from the AS 209 gas giant protoplanet candidate, a gap of approximately 5.5 AU. Using high-resolution ALMA observations, we analyzed the continuum and $^{12}$CO emission within the candidate gap, revealing a significant decrease in gas mass fraction compared to neighboring regions. This anomaly could be the signature of mass accumulation, suggesting gas accretion and planetary formation. Alternatively, it might result from other mechanisms such as dust growth, sublimation or chemical transformations. Comparing gas and dust properties, we found that dust is more clumped than solid material, indicating the presence of unseen mass. However, it is essential to consider other explanations, such as mass accumulation, accretion and planetary formation.

To make the most out of time-sensitive experiments, an effective analysis is crucial for gaining clear understanding of underlying phenomena, which in turn drives further research advancements. However, processing large amounts of time-sensitive data comes with its own set of challenges, such as writing efficient code and setting up automated analysis systems, that even experienced analysts find difficult to manage. In an attempt to simplify this process, our team developed a comprehensive software suite based on a Python script known as boxox, originally created for analyzing time-sensitive data from the MAX IV storage ring, and have now made the entire suite freely accessible online for anyone to utilize.

This paper investigates the concept of mild solutions for first-order mean field games featuring control measures, constraints on the state variable, and a canonical flow with canonical restriction. A key result shows that a mean field game solution can be found when certain conditions are met, even if those conditions are minimal.

We have developed a novel approach to uncovering stellar filaments in the Milky Way. Utilizing the significant Gaia DR2 dataset, which comprises approximately 2 million stars within 2.5 kpc of the Sun, our method identifies clusters of collinear stars that connect to form a network of star-forming structures within the Galaxy's disk plane. This network consists of several distinct systems: the dense core near the Galactic center connected to the outer dotsonic structure beyond 1.5 kpc; the concentrated stellar pattern within the Orizonal Polar Circle; and the scattered stellar distribution within the Northern Galactic Hemisphere. Our analysis sheds new light on the origins and connections of these structures. To further explore the phenomena, we plan to expand our study using the upcoming Gaia EDR3 dataset, which will contain over 1 billion stars.

This research focuses on identifying visual incompatibilities in clothing items, extending previous work on body part-based garment segmentation to cover various types of clothing. To achieve accurate visual incompatibility detection, a new approach is proposed, combining a Fashion contrastive pre-training method, a Vision and Text encoder, and a contrastive loss function. Unlike previous contrastive pre-training on clothing items, which were often based on unrelated datasets, such as INDR, our approach pre-trains with the Labeled Fashion Products (LFP) dataset, specifically tailored for clothing. Experimental results on two real-world datasets, VISW and TFB, demonstrate the effectiveness of our identified visual incompatibilities, with additional analysis provided for the VISW dataset.

This study offers a comprehensive exploration of the resource framework for standardizing broadened classical behaviors through the method of generalized illumination. Firstly, we define the characteristics of enhanced non-classical behavior and establish a reliable criterion for distinguishing it. Subsequently, we outline a systematic approach for constructing the complete set of transformations that preserve classical behavior and develop a resource model based on this framework. Lastly, we apply this theory to several practical scenarios, including standard quantum mechanics and higher-dimensional classical systems, demonstrating their relationship with existing resource models.

In federated learning, clients and server cooperate in an interactive process. The server sends model parameters to clients, then receives updated models, and this process repeats. Typically, clients are restricted from changing models after they are received, but in this paper, we allow them to modify models as they please, as long as they are received, in exchange for a more realistic representation of asynchronous federated learning. To address the clients' asynchronous operations and avoid clients waiting too long, we use a buffer to aggregate updates at the server, one at a time, instead of trying to gather updates from multiple clients at once. Instead of using fixed time intervals to collect updates, the server actively decides when to collect updates to minimize the total time spent waiting. Our results show that this Unrestricted FED+BA approach works well in theory and performs better than other methods on async federated learning in terms of convergence, consistency of final models and efficiency.

This study delves into the linear space of polynomials, denoted by $\mathcal{P}$, within a broader mathematical framework, the space of tempered distributions, and examines its role as a subset of various distribution spaces. Building on established foundations, we define a specific topology on $\mathcal{P}$, proving its equivalence to the uniform convergence topology in compact sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Fourier transform serves as an isomorphism between $(\mathcal{P}', E)$ and $(\mathcal{P}, E)$, effectively linking the dual space of polynomials, used in mean periodic functions, to the study of polynomials themselves.

A three-dimensional duality between de Sitter space and black holes suggests that dark energy might be linked to black holes. We found that this connection holds true, and dark energy's density could be contributed to by dark matter. Specifically, this connection applies to dark matter fractions comprised of small primordial black holes. Because these black holes are stored in the extra dimension, they don't interact with the visible world until they're released from it, during which time their density adds to the dark energy. Since dark matter in our observable universe is in equilibrium with dark energy, the dark matter fraction of these small black holes remains constant. This finding implies that dark energy is fundamentally connected to black holes.

Biological membranes are largely comprised of a lipid bilayer that forms the basic structure of cells. Despite their apparent simplicity, membranes exhibit complex and dynamic properties stemming from the diverse shapes and interactions of constituent lipids. Recent research suggests that phase boundaries, or gaps, within membranes play a crucial role in shaping cell physiology and influencing cellular processes. Here, we introduce a theoretical framework to investigate the physical characteristics of phase boundaries, focusing on specific lipid models and examining the underlying long-range interactions. Using this analytical approach, we identify key indicators for detecting gaps and provide a method to quantify their width.

The wide-bandgap property of GaN is desirable for enhancing photon damage resistance and reducing leakage current in GaN transistors. Recent advances suggest that ternary nitrides such as ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ have a lattice constant that could potentially match GaN's. However, the electronic effects of matching these lattices are yet to be confirmed experimentally. Our study demonstrates that matching GaN's lattice to that of ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ enhances its electronic properties, specifically the hole conductivity, by approximately two orders of magnitude. InGa$x$N$_{1-x}$GaxN$_2$ and Ga$_{1-x}$Mg$_x$N compounds exhibit this enhanced electronic behavior, exhibiting a low activation energy, thereby potentially enabling the modulation of GaN's hole conductivity. The increased hole conductivity is attributed to the increased valence band position, shifted from -5.8 eV to -3.8 eV relative to the GaN valence band, resulting in increased effective hole masses in the range of 0.025-0.045 m$_e$. Our results are consistent with the proposed mechanisms and can aid in the optical and electrical activation of GaN's. The increased hole conductivity may enable the lattice matching to reduce GaN's photon sensitivity and improve its hole injection for enhancing hole blocking diodes.

Several advanced path planning strategies, such as Rapidly-exploring Random Trees and Veracite Robot Learning, rely on heuristic policies rather than optimisation. In contrast, Option Framework-based strategies can learn more effective policies through demonstration. However, these learned policies require significant computational resources. To address this challenge, our research focuses on learning sparse guidance functions using Gaussian Process Time Difference learning, enabling more efficient long-term planning. By leveraging temporal difference training and sparse approximation, our approach minimises the time needed to find optimal actions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a marine robot by comparing its performance to other planning strategies and showing that it produces comparable results while requiring significantly fewer computations.

We examine isothermic surfaces in 3D Euclidean space that have meromorphic properties. We demonstrate how to extend isothermic surfaces that have singularities along a curve. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the Darboux and Calapso transformations of isothermic surfaces. By using the framework of loop groups, we establish the mapping of these transformations. The findings are then applied to isothermic Hopf surfaces.

We introduce and analyze a nonparametric technique for estimating a functional operator that relates a random variable Y to the expectation of a function of y and Y, denoted as F(E[F(y) | Y = y]). This method aims to facilitate the analysis of the effect of a system's state y on its dynamics, as seen in studies of nonlinear dynamical systems and time series analysis. Our approach bypasses the need to make assumptions about the nature of these effects and employs kernel smoothing to estimate the operator. Our analysis demonstrates that under certain conditions, the estimate converges at a rate of n^(-1/2 | log(n)/h(n))), where n represents the sample size and h(n) is the kernel bandwidth. Moreover, we derive an alternative approach for choosing an optimal bandwidth h(n) that maximizes the minimum distance to zero of the estimated operator. Our method is further applied to estimate the Lyapunov spectrum of a nonlinear system and the direction of the leading eigenfunction. Our simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in identifying bifurcations in simple nonlinear systems and using greedy algorithms to reduce high-dimensional dynamical systems.

This paper explores the properties of λ-analogues of r-Stirling numbers of the second kind through a new defined polynomial and a related identity. It also presents a λ-Soper identity with an alternative formulation. Moreover, it establishes identities involving λ-analogues of r-Stirling numbers of the second kind with variable values.

Temporal knowledge graph linking considers how entities are related both temporally and conceptually, where static linking models outperform their static-temporal counterparts on average. Nevertheless, some static models can be adapted to temporal settings by outmatching their specialized equivalents.

C* algebras arising from finite graphs can be characterized by their generating graphs, which are considered robust if they have finite covers that are also valid for the algebras. C* algebras of finite graphs are shift equivalent to each other under robust shift equivalence if there are finite, strongly connected graphs that are shift equivalent to their corresponding infinite graphs, and their associated C* algebras are isomorphic. A key finding in this area is that the robust equivalence classes of finite graph C* algebras are finite in number.

In intense magnetic fields, the movement of charged particles is constrained within a flat elliptical path, and their interactions with other particles result in distinct ejection paths based on the charge to mass ratio. Simulations of the quark-gluon plasma at finite magnetic field strength have shown that the interaction between bottom quarks and light quarks leads to distinct propagator behaviors. These behaviors can be used in tomography techniques to reconstruct properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Our study utilized the retarded correlator of general propagators at strong magnetic fields and found that the difference in real and imaginary parts can be used to Anisotropy tomography. This technique is more sensitive than the method employed in previous studies and can detect the degradation of quark-gluon plasma. Additionally, we found that this method is less susceptible to numerical noise. Our results indicate that the Anisotropy of the propagator's imaginary part can be used for tomography of the quark-gluon plasma.

Natural language question answering is significantly complicated by linguistic nuances, such as word ambiguity, sentence structure, and semantic relationships, especially when encountering novel data. Leveraging knowledge graphs for reasoning can help resolve these challenges and improve understanding of language, although current methods are limited to simple tasks. This research undertakes an in-depth evaluation of integrating knowledge graphs for reasoning in question answering, particularly in handling complex queries involving relational paths. Following this investigation, a new graph-neural-network-based model is proposed to demonstrate the practical value of our findings.

Cover-based extenders are widely used methods for generating sequences with low cross-correlation. In particular, they play a crucial role in creating sequences with novel properties using techniques such as modulo addition and bitwise XOR. Given the constraints imposed by existing bounds in higher dimensions, there's a pressing need for new methods to overcome these limitations. This study presents four methods for constructing new extenders in higher dimensions, some of which result in novel examples of non-existent objects such as constant weight orthogonal arrays with certain parameters. A comprehensive list of existing two-dimensional extenders is also provided for easy reference.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential of context-dependent prompts to accurately solve tasks we have not been explicitly trained on. Our research delves into the effectiveness of prompts in multiple choice tasks, focusing on three main questions. Firstly, we investigate if there are certain multiple choice tasks that can be solved without prior training. Our tests across eight such tasks show that some can be solved without prior training, but others prove challenging. Our analysis reveals that tasks with overlapping choices and limited relevant options are difficult to solve. Secondly, we examine the influence of prompt design on model performance. Our findings indicate that including the question text in the context improves performance compared to prompts that merely list the available options. Additionally, including the correct answer in the context significantly boosts model accuracy. Lastly, we investigate the role of models in multiple choice tasks. Our results across eight models show that GPT-3 excels compared to other models, but all models struggle with tasks that lack relevant questions and overlap in the available options.

We have computed the $\mathscr L$-invariants associated with Artin symbols within a specific context, namely when an odd irreducible polynomial $f$ and an odd prime $p$ are involved. The symbols represent a two-dimensional Galois representation with coefficients in the algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q_\p$ and we employ Mazur's theory to analyze its behavior. By completing this representation at certain infinite places of the field $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{f+1})$, ultimately determined by the choice of one of these completions, invariants were defined. These completions can be expressed through generalized Bernoulli numbers, ultimately leading to explicit formulas for the $\mathscr L$-invariants.

Achieving precise identification of Rydberg atoms' complex microwave signals across multiple frequencies is a significant challenge. Traditional methods face difficulties in extracting key features from signals and modeling their temporal relationships, resulting in low recognition accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a novel deep learning approach, where a convolutional neural network analyzes signal features and a long short-term recurrent neural network model their relationships to classify frequencies. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method yields superior performance, with a total recognition accuracy of 99.6% and individual frequency accuracies exceeding 99.5%.

UGC 8839, a nearby spiral galaxy without a prominent bar, exhibits two distinct disk structures when analyzed through photometry. Utilizing a dynamical model incorporating a halo, we discover that the inner disk is a thin, stable structure with high dynamic stability, whereas the inner and outer disks are dynamically incompatible in a barless configuration. Our model suggests that the inner disk is a rich source of light in multiple wavelength bands, playing a significant role in the total light of the galaxy across various wavelengths, particularly contributing to the total light in several wavelength bands.

This study demonstrates that the $\mathcal{H}^{s}$-measure of the $k$-stable manifold at point $x$, denoted as $W^{s}_{k}(x)$, is either $0$ or $\infty$ for points $x$ within the Julia set $J(f)$ of a quaseregular mapping $f$: $ \mathbb{R}^{n+1} \rightarrow \mathbb{ quasiregular} mapping \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Specifically, when the mapping degree of $f$ equals one, and the Hausdorff dimension of $J(f)$ exceeds $k$, the $k$-stable manifold at any point $x$ in $J(f)$ has a precisely defined Hausdorff measure by utilizing Parson's theorem. Moreover, when the Hausdorff dimension of $J(f)$ equals $k$, and the mapping degree of $f$ equals one, it follows from verifying the Ahlfors-regular condition by applying Parson's theorem that the $k$-stable manifolds at any point $x$ in $J(f)$ are precisely covered by a family of $(k-1)$-dimensional quasiregular curves, and the convergence of these curves to a quasicircle can be observed.

Using data from MGS, ODY, MRO, and MAVEN, the topographic and gravity waves in the thermosphere of Mars were detected. Their height of penetration reaches as high as 140 km above the surface, primarily driven by the thermosphere's compression caused by these waves. MGS provided the first measurements, spanning 10 years from 2001 to 2011, primarily during the northern spring. In contrast, ODY recorded mostly southern spring data in 2007 and 2008. Furthermore, MRO measured mostly northern spring through 2019 and ODY through 2021 as of now. Both MRO and MAVEN waves were seen to increase their penetration height with rising temperatures. Moreover, in ODY and MAVEN observations, the waves' properties were found to change with seasons. In contrast to Earth, where MWs are amplified by magnetic forces, evidence suggests that GWs in Mars were primarily caused by gravity.

The LHC has discovered that ultra-peripheral heavy-ion and proton-nucleus collisions have powerful photon sources with extraordinary properties. These collisions, particularly those involving lead ions, are driven by large, low-frequency photons that can trigger both electromagnetic and photon-photon interactions. Recent experiments using the ALICE detector at a 5.2 TeV Nucleon-Nucleon energy have examined J/psi production in such collisions. By comparing these results to those from peripheral collisions and central collisions, scientists aim to investigate how photons in ultra-peripheral collisions interact with each other and with bound quarks within the lead ions. This analysis is informed by theoretical models and data from electromagnetic processes at lower energies. The ALICE collaboration recently published its findings on J/psi production in ultra-peripheral Pb-Pb collisions in addition to measuring forward J/psi production in ultra-peripheral Pb-Pb, and central Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV.

In line with recent advancements in audio-visual synthesis, we strive to improve the quality of sound by leveraging visual cues. Existing methods primarily employ a straightforward sampling technique from a pre-trained neural model, which often results in incoherent noises. To address this limitation, we've developed a novel approach that utilizes the information from better-quality samples to guide pre-trained models in generating more visually aligned high-fidelity sounds. Specifically, we've designed a fine-grained, phoneme-based refinement framework that mimics the characteristics of low-fidelity noises. The framework's effectiveness will be demonstrated through extensive experiments on both synthetic and natural image datasets.

Recurrent Neural Networks have emerged as leading candidates in addressing complex sequence-based problems across various domains, such as text, speech, and music. Despite their success, recurrent neural networks pose challenges in training and optimization. In response to the surge in applications requiring processing of sequential data, this article aims to provide an in-depth examination of recurrent neural networks, showcasing their use cases and underlying principles, and to discuss key issues in their implementation.

Our approach aligns with existing research in modeling pandemic dynamics under specific assumptions, however, our analytical method超越了 most models by offering precise solutions rather than approximate ones. We've determined that early adoption of non-pharmaceutical interventions combined with rapid response times can minimize overall economic and health losses. Furthermore, our findings indicate that timely implementation of these interventions has minimal impact on model predictions, even when considering real-world factors, and that these results hold across a wide range of underlying models.

Data science projects often face the complex task of data science debugging. 
An effective approach to streamline this process involves integrating explainable AI techniques, such as Shapley values, into the workflow. 
A custom open-source tool, SigShary, has been developed to simplify the process of applying Shapley values to various machine learning frameworks and pipelines, enabling users to visually analyze its output and effectively debug their data science projects. 
By incorporating SigShary, users can gain valuable insights and achieve a better understanding of their machine learning models and the data used to train them.

This informal introduction to the topic focuses on meaning-preserving transformations of degree one, specifically within the context of extremal metrics on hidden geometric structures. These extremal metrics hold significant value in addressing fundamental problems within the field of Kähler geometry, with extensive implications.

manganese based triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn exhibits various magnetic phases at low temperatures, including an anomalous Hall effect at room temperature when magnetic fields are applied parallel to the material's atomic layers. This anomalous Hall effect can surpass the Hall effect in highly doped semiconductors, even in the absence of long range order. Recent studies have shown that the anomalous Hall effect can be triggered by manipulating spin waves or weak magnetic fields, yet the material still retains a finite value at zero temperature. We have discovered that both a pressure of 3.5 kilobars and a temperature of 150 Kelvin can induce the anomalous Hall effect at 1 Tesla. Notably, we have found that the anomalous Hall coefficient at 1 Tesla, 300 Kelvin, and under pressure, reaches 160 percent of its unpressurized value. This suggests that pressure stabilizes a magnetically ordered state on the material's atomic layers, and we have confirmed this through a study of lattice and electronic changes. This finding paves the way for developing new devices that utilize topological multiferroic materials.

Extracting abstract connections between words in texts has long been pursued in NLP, particularly through the identification of terms related to specific entities, such as those found within a knowledge base. However, conventional methods often require manual annotation and are constrained by predefined vocabularies. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing deep neural networks to automate connection identification without these limitations. Notably, this deep learning-based method can handle entities beyond predefined terms and phrases, as well as terms that are not initially part of a limited vocabulary.

This paper delves into a specific problem involving the Steklov-Robin spectrum of a bounded domain in n-dimensional space. We have proven the existence of a sequence of Steklov-Robin eigenfunctions whose corresponding L^2-norms tend to zero at an accelerated rate, as the index of the eigenfunctions goes to infinity. Under the assumption that coefficients are variable, we also demonstrate the non-existence of eigenfunctions belonging to certain high-order Sobolev spaces.

Rebuilding hypergraphs from their sample data is a key challenge in graph analysis. In recent years, some approaches have emerged, such as using density information in the embedding to identify k-cliques as sample points move towards the graph's core. However, this method struggles when dealing with sparse graphs, those that have been randomly generated, or those that contain many edges. To address this issue, we propose a new hypergraph reconstruction method that takes into account a hypergraph's structural properties. Using the fractal dimension of the graph, we develop an algorithm to identify its key parameters. Extensive testing on both real-world and artificially created graphs has demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach.

In medical education and clinical practice, chest radiographs (CXR) are extensively employed, but their limited 2D spatial resolution and language barriers can lead to misdiagnosis and misinterpretations by physicians. Radiologists often rely on complementary computed tomography (CT) scans to confirm CXR diagnoses, but teaching health professionals to decipher radiological findings by merely examining CXRs remains a difficult task. This study developed a CXR annotation protocol, utilizing projections from corresponding CT scans, to provide more precise and comprehensive findings that align with those obtained from CT scans. Furthermore, this dataset, consisting of 153 patient cases and 515 findings, along with the associated findings report, serves to advance the fields of radiological report parsing and medical question answering. The dataset can also enhance the capabilities of question answering models specifically tailored for CXRs, through its paired search and diagnostic reports.

Euler characteristics of tight contact structures on certain three-dimensional manifolds with boundary are determined by the Thurston norm of a specific class of two-dimensional surfaces, specifically those that closely mirror the underlying manifold's structure. These Euler characteristics can be organized into linear functions, which depend on the Euler characteristic and geodesic length of two-dimensional, genus $g$ surfaces, where the geometric properties of these surfaces are measured using the metric of the manifold's cone over the boundary. Our method involves computing specific areas associated with these surfaces, which are related to their geometric lengths, and this computation can be performed using techniques such as polyhedral decompositions.

One key issue in the development of on-chip lasers revolves around excessive heat buildup. Examine the potential benefits of microcavity lasers that emit light in a single direction using two-dimensional photonic crystal structures featuring line defects. Through 3D numerical simulations, we found the entropy of emitted photons in these structures is substantially higher compared to conventional diffraction-based lasers, yielding better overall efficiency.

Our research validates the suitability of cryptocurrencies for transactions due to their stability in value. To achieve this, we contrasted major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Litecoin, with traditional commodities like gold, silver, and crude oil, as well as equity indexes, using statistical metrics such as returns, volatility, and correlations. Additionally, we applied the mean absolute deviation and K\"{a}hler value stability indices to quantify value stability, finding that Bitcoin demonstrates the highest stability among all cryptocurrencies and is comparable to gold, silver, and crude oil. Furthermore, Bitcoin's performance becomes even more pronounced in the context of tradeable amounts, reinforcing its potential as a medium of exchange.

We verify a scaling limit of the exact solution formula derived through the Riemann-Hilbert approach, which describes the distribution of maximum heights at large times or distances in the one-dimensional Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation. Our analysis reveals that for large $\beta \gg 1$, the distribution can be modeled as a Gamma distribution, characterized by parameters that depend on the respective parameters of the exact solution formula.
